notes.34:2: Chapters 33–35 in the Septuagint correspond to chapters 26–28 in the Hebrew Bible; chapter 34 is substantially shorter in the Greek text, lacking counterparts to MT 27:1, 7, 13, 17, and 21.
notes.34:3: Greek Idoumaia ("Idumea") is the Septuagint's regular name for Edom, and the phrase "who come to meet them" reflects a distinct Greek reading.
notes.34:11: Greek reads "and it shall serve him" (referring to the king of Babylon), whereas the Hebrew refers to tilling the land ("and it shall till it").
notes.34:18: Greek apantesatosan moi ("let them meet Me") continues first-person divine speech from verse 16, whereas the Hebrew reads "let them intercede with the Lord of hosts."
notes.35:3: Greek "Yet two years of days" literally renders the Hebrew idiom for two full years.
notes.35:13: Greek reads the first-person future poieso ("I will make"), attributing the iron yoke-bars directly to the Lord, whereas the Hebrew reads the second-person "you have made."
notes.35:15: Greek ep' adiko ("in what is unjust") renders the Hebrew term for falsehood with moral terminology, consistent with adika and ep' adiko in 34:14–16.
notes.36:1: The Greek text specifies "false prophets" (ψευδοπροφήτας) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text (29:1) has "prophets," and places "a letter to Babylon for the exiles" in apposition to "the words of the book."
notes.36:11: The Greek text is significantly briefer than the Hebrew (29:11), reading "a purpose of peace and not evil things, to give these things to you" without "a future and a hope"; verses 16-20 of the Hebrew are also absent from the Septuagint.
notes.36:24: The Greek text identifies Shemaiah as "the Elamite" (τὸν Αἰλαμείτην) where the Hebrew (29:24) reads "the Nehelamite"; the same proper name recurs in verse 31.
notes.36:25: The Greek reads "I did not send you in My name. And to Zephaniah... say," diverging sharply from the Hebrew (29:25), which accuses Shemaiah of sending letters in his own name; likewise, verse 27 omits the negative ("why have you reviled" rather than "why have you not rebuked").
notes.37:6: The Greek contains the distinct clause "and concerning fear in which they shall hold fast their loins and deliverance," and uses ἴκτερος ("jaundice") for the sickly pallor of terrified faces.
notes.37:12: The Greek opens with a first-person declaration by the Lord, "I have raised up a fracture" (Ἀνέστησα σύντριμμα), where the Hebrew (30:12) reads "Your hurt is incurable"; verses 10-11, 15, and 22 of the Hebrew are absent from the Septuagint.
notes.37:16: The Greek reads "all your enemies shall eat all their own flesh" where the Hebrew (30:16) has "all your adversaries shall go into captivity," and includes the clause "because of the multitude of your iniquities..." within this verse.
notes.37:17: The Greek renders "She is your prey" (θήρευμα ὑμῶν ἐστίν) where the Hebrew (30:17) reads "It is Zion"; similarly, verse 18 reads "captivity" and "the people" for Hebrew "tents" and "palace," and verse 20 reads "testimonies" for "congregation."
notes.38:2: The Greek reads "warmth" (thermon) and "go, and do not destroy Israel," differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("found grace... when Israel went to seek rest").
notes.38:8: The Greek reads "at the feast of Passover" (transliterating the Hebrew word as phasek), where the Masoretic Text reads "among them the blind and the lame."
notes.38:22: The Septuagint reads "the Lord has created salvation for a new planting; in salvation men shall walk about," a markedly different reading from the Masoretic Text ("a woman shall encompass a man").
notes.38:32: The Greek reads "and I disregarded them" (echoed in Hebrews 8:9), where the Masoretic Text reads "though I was a husband to them."
notes.38:38: The Greek reads the proper name "Hanameel" (Hanameel) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has "Hananel."
notes.38:40: "Asaremoth" (transliterated from a Hebrew term for fields or terraces) and "Nahal Kidron" (transliterating Hebrew nachal, "brook" or "wadi") preserve the Septuagint's own Greek transliterations.
notes.39:8: The Greek text spells Hanamel's father's name Samol here (a metathesis of Shallum in v. 7), and adds "and you are the elder" (presbyteros), indicating seniority in the right of redemption.
notes.39:14: Where the Masoretic Text speaks of "the open deed," the Greek reads to anegnosmenon ("the scroll that was read"), referring to the unsealed copy available for public reading.
notes.39:15: The Greek reads ktisthēsontai ("shall be established/built," from ktizō), differing from the Masoretic Text's "shall be bought" (cf. ktēthēsontai in v. 43).
notes.39:17: The divine address Ho ōn Kyrie ("O Lord, the One who is") echoes the Greek of Exodus 3:14 (ho ōn) in rendering the Hebrew exclamation of prayer.
notes.39:39: The Greek reads "another way and another heart" (hodon heteran kai kardian heteran), contrasting with the Masoretic Text's "one heart and one way."
notes.40:6: The Greek places "and I will reveal to them" before "and I will heal it," followed by "both peace and faithfulness," preserving an unusual clause order compared to the Masoretic Text.
notes.40:9: The Greek reads pikranthēsontai ("they shall be embittered") where the Masoretic Text has "they shall tremble."
notes.40:10: The Greek translates the Hebrew word for "streets" as exōthen ("outside Jerusalem").
notes.40:13: The Septuagint text of this chapter ends at verse 13, lacking the royal and Levitical covenant promises found in Masoretic Text Jeremiah 33:14-26.
notes.41:5: The Septuagint reads "wept / shall weep" and "even to Hades they shall lament for you," differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's reference to burning spices and crying "Alas, lord!"
notes.41:10: The Septuagint condenses verses 10–11 into a single sentence split across the verse boundary; the verb rendered "forced" (ἐῶσαν) reflects an aorist form of ὠθέω ("compel/thrust"), though it may also be read as a Koine form of ἐάω ("left/kept").
notes.41:14: The Septuagint specifies "six years" rather than the seven years found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.41:18: The Septuagint reads "the calf which they made to serve it," differing markedly from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's reference to cutting the calf in two and passing between its parts.
notes.41:21: The final clause is elliptical in Greek ("and the army of the king of Babylon for those who flee from them"), reflecting a difficult rendering of the Hebrew reference to the retreating Babylonian army.
notes.42:2: "Archabein" (Ἁρχαβείν) is the Septuagint's distinct Greek form for the house of the Rechabites (incorporating the Hebrew definite article), whereas "Rechab" (Ῥηχάβ) appears in verse 6 and following.
notes.42:3: The Septuagint preserves distinct proper names in verses 3–4, including "Jeconiah the son of Jeremin, the son of Chabasein" (vs. MT Jaazaniah son of Jeremiah son of Habazziniah) and "Jonan the son of Hananiah, the son of Gedaliah" (vs. MT Hanan son of Igdaliah).
notes.42:11: The Septuagint reads "the Assyrians" (Ἀσσυρίων) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "the Arameans" (Syrians).
notes.42:18: Unlike the Hebrew Masoretic Text, the Septuagint omits a narrative transition introducing Jeremiah's address to the Rechabites, continues directly in the third person, and adds "of the earth" at the end of verse 19.
notes.43:9: The Greek text reads "in the eighth year," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text (Jer 36:9) reads "in the fifth year."
notes.43:14: The Greek text omits the messenger Jehudi here and attaches the lineage "the son of Nethaniah, the son of Shelemiah, the son of Cushi" directly to Baruch the son of Neriah.
notes.43:20: The Greek text reads "Elisha" here and in verse 21, differing from "Elishama" in verse 12.
notes.43:25: The Greek text names "Elnathan and Gedaliah" and states that they advised the king to burn the scroll, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text (Jer 36:25) lists Elnathan, Delaiah, and Gemariah urging him not to burn it.
notes.43:26: The Greek text reads "they hid themselves" without specifying an agent, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text (Jer 36:26) states that the Lord hid them.
notes.44:5: The Greek text literally reads "went up against Jerusalem," differing from verse 11 and the Hebrew Masoretic Text (Jer 37:5), which state that the Chaldeans departed from Jerusalem.
notes.44:12: The Greek text reads "to buy from there," differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text (Jer 37:12), which refers to receiving a portion among the people.
notes.44:13: The Greek text identifies the man as "a man with whom he lodged" and names him "Saruia," differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text (Jer 37:13), which refers to "a captain of the guard" named "Irijah."
notes.44:16: "Chereth" transliterates Greek chereth, which renders a Hebrew term for vaulted dungeon cells.
notes.44:20: Greek literally reads "let my mercy fall before your face" (an idiom for a plea for mercy, as in 43:7) and phrases the following clause as a question ("why do you send me back...").
notes.45:1: "Saphanias the son of Nathan" follows the Greek text directly, where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "Shephatiah the son of Mattan" and also includes "Pashhur the son of Malchijah."
notes.45:4: "prophesy" translates the rare Greek verb chresimologeo, meaning to speak beneficially or prophesy good.
notes.45:9: The Greek addresses the king directly ("You have done wickedly in what you have done"), whereas the Hebrew text blames the officials who cast Jeremiah into the cistern.
notes.45:14: "Aseleisel" is the Septuagint transliteration of a Hebrew phrase meaning "the third [entrance]."
notes.45:27: "because the word of the Lord was not heard" preserves the Septuagint reading; the Hebrew text reads "for the matter was not overheard."
notes.46:1: "in the ninth month of Zedekiah" follows the Greek text directly, where the Hebrew text specifies "in the ninth year of Zedekiah, in the tenth month."
notes.46:3: The Greek preserves distinct forms for the Babylonian officials' names and titles (Marganasar, Samagoth, Nabusachar, Nabusareis, Nagargasnaser, Rabamath). In the Septuagint, verse 14 follows immediately after verse 3, without verses 4-13 of the Hebrew text (Jeremiah 39:4-13).
notes.46:18: "for a prize" translates Greek heurema ("a find" or "windfall"), rendering the Hebrew idiom "as spoil," signifying that his life would be spared.
notes.47:1: "captain of the guard" renders Greek archimageiros (literally "chief cook"), the standard Septuagint title for the royal bodyguard commander; "Daman" preserves the Greek place name, where the Hebrew text reads "Ramah."
notes.47:8: "Jophe" preserves the distinct Greek form of the name, corresponding to "Ephai" in the Hebrew text.
notes.47:9: "the servants of the Chaldeans" follows the Septuagint reading, whereas the Hebrew text reads "to serve the Chaldeans."
notes.47:11: "Idumea" preserves the Septuagint Greek name for the land of Edom.
notes.48:1: Greek reads "Elasa," whereas the Masoretic Text (Jeremiah 41:1) reads "Elishama."
notes.48:5: Greek reads "Salem" (for Masoretic "Shiloh") and "manna" (a Greek transliteration of the Hebrew term for a grain offering), and describes the men as "beating their breasts" rather than gashing themselves.
notes.48:6: Greek states that the pilgrims ("they") were walking along and weeping, whereas the Masoretic Text describes Ishmael as weeping as he went out.
notes.48:17: Greek reads the place-name "Gaberochamaa," corresponding to "Geruth Chimham" in the Masoretic Text (Jeremiah 41:17).
notes.49:1: Greek reads "Azariah the son of Maaseiah," whereas the Masoretic Text (Jeremiah 42:1) reads "Jezaniah the son of Hoshaiah."
notes.49:12: Greek keeps all three verbs in the first person ("I will grant... I will have mercy... I will bring you back"), making the Lord the direct subject rather than the king of Babylon as in the Masoretic Text.
notes.49:17: Greek includes "and all the foreigners" among those setting their faces toward Egypt, a phrase not present in the Masoretic Text.
notes.49:18: Greek renders the judgment terms as "an untrodden waste, and in subjection," diverging from "an execration and an astonishment" in the Masoretic Text.
notes.50:9: Greek reads "in the entranceway" (en prothyrois), whereas the Masoretic Text (Jeremiah 43:9) reads "in the mortar in the brick pavement."
notes.50:10: Greek reads "which you have hidden" and "he shall lift up his weapons against them," whereas the Masoretic Text has "which I have hidden" and "he will spread his royal canopy over them."
notes.50:12: Greek uses the vivid verb phtheirizo ("delouse"), picturing Nebuchadnezzar stripping Egypt clean as a shepherd picks lice from his garment, whereas the Masoretic Text speaks of wrapping himself in the land.
notes.50:13: Greek specifies "Heliopolis that are in On," using the Greek name for the Egyptian city of the sun alongside its Hebrew name On, whereas the Masoretic Text reads "Beth-shemesh in the land of Egypt."
notes.51:1: In the Septuagint order of Jeremiah, chapter 51 comprises the oracles corresponding to chapters 44 (verses 1-30) and 45 (verses 31-35) of the Masoretic Text.
notes.51:21: The Greek uses the first-person plural 'which we burned,' though the appositive list immediately shifts to the second person, 'you and your fathers.'
notes.51:25: Unlike the Masoretic Text, which addresses both the men and their wives, the Greek directs this rebuke specifically to 'you women' using feminine participles throughout.
notes.51:33: The Greek reads 'I lay down in groanings,' whereas the Masoretic Text reads 'I am weary with my groaning.'
notes.52:4: The Greek dates the start of the siege to 'the ninth month' (Masoretic Text: 'the tenth month'), describes the siege works as 'four-footed,' and omits verses 2-3, 15, and 28-30 found in the Masoretic Text.
notes.52:9: The Greek reads 'Deblatha' here and in verses 10, 26, and 27 (Masoretic Text: 'Riblah'), and in verse 11 places Zedekiah in 'the millhouse' (Masoretic Text: 'the prison').
notes.52:12: 'Chief cook' literally renders the Greek title archimageiros, the Septuagint's standard equivalent for the Babylonian captain of the royal guard.
notes.52:19: The Greek retains two transliterated Hebrew terms for temple utensils, 'sapphoth' (likely basins or bowls) and 'masmaroth' (likely snuffers or forks).
notes.52:21: The Greek gives the height of each pillar as 'thirty-five cubits' (matching 2 Chronicles 3:15; Masoretic Text: 'eighteen cubits') and adds 'eight pomegranates to a cubit for the twelve cubits' in verse 22.
notes.52:31: The Greek names the exiled king 'Jehoiakim' (Masoretic Text: 'Jehoiachin') and the Babylonian king 'Ulaimadachar' (Masoretic Text: 'Evil-Merodach'), dates the release to 'the twenty-fourth day' (Masoretic Text: 'twenty-fifth'), and adds that he 'shaved him.'
